messages.author: 275b133a3506805a
messages.subject: Kalman filter in Stan
parts:
Dear all,

Still learning Stan, so working up a very simple example, a 1D Kalman filter:
<https://github.com/danstowell/kalman1dstan>

When I run it with default options, the mean of the samples doesn't
give me a very good estimate of the parameters. (True parameter values
are in makedata.py.) The f_trans seems to come out close enough, but
the others, not great. Any advice please?

Dan
--
http://www.mcld.co.uk

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Kalman filter in Stan
parts:
Please take this with a grain of salt, because I'm not
that familiar with Kalman filters. There are some
general issues with the model, though.

1. You have improper uniform priors on all of the regression
coefficients and noise terms. And on x[1]. Putting priors
on these helps dampen the huge amount of posterior certainty
in this model.

2. The model does not seem to be identifiable as specified. Changing
the sign of both x and h_trans leads to the same results. Constraining
h_trans to be positive seems to help. But there still seems to be a huge
amount of posterior uncertainty.

3. Is it OK to have a ftrans = -1.01? It implies an
oscillation around f_off in the x[n] because

x[n] ~ normal(f_off + f_trans * x[n-1], f_noise);

I've attached a simulator in R, as well as a revised model

with much stronger priors and a positivity constraint on h_trans.

4. Even if I constrain f_trans and h_trans to be between 0 and 1
and remove h_off and f_off from the model, there's still a huge
degree of posterior uncerainty.

Part of the problem may be that 100 data points isn't enough
to estimate this model well because of the degrees of freedom.

I used a non-diagonal mass matrix, but that doesn't seem
to make much of a difference.

The model could also be vectorized for speed.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Kalman filter in Stan
parts:
Bob,

Thanks.

2013/6/13 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>:

> Please take this with a grain of salt, because I'm not
> that familiar with Kalman filters.

Actually in this context it's just a shorthand for a time-series model
with Gaussian updates and Gaussian observations - not much extra to be
familiar with. Also, in the typical Kalman filter, the
update/observation parameters are hard-coded, whereas here I was
hoping to infer them - too optimistic.

> There are some
> general issues with the model, though.
>
> 1. You have improper uniform priors on all of the regression
> coefficients and noise terms. And on x[1]. Putting priors
> on these helps dampen the huge amount of posterior certainty
> in this model.

Thanks. Wanted to leave priors on the coefficients improper (to see if
it would work anyway), but that's nonsense for the noise terms in
particular since the hidden time series needs _some_ kind of anchoring
to the observations.

> 2. The model does not seem to be identifiable as specified. Changing
> the sign of both x and h_trans leads to the same results. Constraining
> h_trans to be positive seems to help. But there still seems to be a huge
> amount of posterior uncertainty.

That positivity constraint is undesirable in general, but yes I do
need to break the symmetry somewhere. I can do this by having an
off-centre prior on h_trans.

> 3. Is it OK to have a ftrans = -1.01? It implies an
> oscillation around f_off in the x[n] because
>
> x[n] ~ normal(f_off + f_trans * x[n-1], f_noise);
Yes, oscillation is fine, and deliberate.

> I've attached a simulator in R, as well as a revised model
> with much stronger priors and a positivity constraint on h_trans.
>
> 4. Even if I constrain f_trans and h_trans to be between 0 and 1
> and remove h_off and f_off from the model, there's still a huge
> degree of posterior uncerainty.
>
> Part of the problem may be that 100 data points isn't enough
> to estimate this model well because of the degrees of freedom.
>
> I used a non-diagonal mass matrix, but that doesn't seem
> to make much of a difference.
>
> The model could also be vectorized for speed.

I don't want it to run fast though. Gives me a chance to catch up ;)

Thanks
Dan

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Kalman filter in Stan
parts:
Roweis and Gharamani (1999) explain these models
and what's needed to identify them:


http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~liam/teaching/neurostat-spr12/papers/hmm/roweis-ghahramani-lds.pdf

The observation noise needs to be set to 1.0 because otherwise
the scale of the coefficient on the observation isn't identified.

So here's a model that works (also attached):

data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector[N] y;
}
parameters {
vector[N] x;
real f_off;
real f_trans;
real h_off;
real h_trans;
real<lower=0> h_noise;
}
model {
f_off ~ normal(0,1);
f_trans ~ normal(0,1);
h_off ~ normal(0,1);
h_trans ~ normal(0,1);
h_noise ~ normal(0,1);

x[1] ~ normal(0,10); // fat prior on x
for (n in 2:N)
x[n] ~ normal(f_off + f_trans * x[n-1], 1);
y ~ normal(h_off + h_trans * x, h_noise);
}

No more constraints on parameters, but the scale of x[2:N] is
fixed to 1; x[1] has a looser prior to deal with initial
conditions.

Here's an example of the simulated values originally supplied
by Dan Stowell (other than f_noise, which is now 1.0):

f_off <- 0.1;
f_trans <- -1.01;
f_noise <- 1.0; # was 0.3; (unit to identify)
h_off <- 1.2;
h_trans <- 0.4;
h_noise <- 0.7;
N <- 100;

Here's what's recovered by Stan (with f_noise set to 1); you can
see the reflection invariance:

f_off -0.1 0.0 0.9 -1.8 -0.7 -0.1 0.6 1.8 369 1
f_trans -1.0 0.0 0.0 -1.0 -1.0 -1.0 -1.0 -0.9 735 1
h_off 1.1 0.0 0.2 0.7 1.0 1.1 1.3 1.6 377 1
h_trans -0.4 0.0 0.1 -0.6 -0.5 -0.4 -0.4 -0.3 145 1
h_noise 0.8 0.0 0.1 0.7 0.8 0.8 0.9 1.0 549 1
lp__ -83.7 0.6 9.6 -103.3 -90.0 -83.6 -77.0 -66.3 240 1

This was with 2500 post-warmup iterations, so effective sample size
still isn't great, but that seems to be the case with most time-series-like
models.

Fitting is still a bit unstable. Without init=0, convergence is
not good.

With 100 data points and fairly tight priors, there's still large
posterior uncertainty.

Going to 1000 data points is problematic. I think this may be partly
due to the simulated x values rising to 1e5 with the exponential
growth due to ftrans=-1.01. With ftrans=0.8, it all fits very
tightly with N=1000.

- Bob
